prompt: Put the steps the interpreter takes when evaluating `"10" > 9` in order.
hint: Before deciding how to compare, something has to be established about the operands. Comparing is the last thing that happens, not the first.
items: Establishes that the operands have different types: a string and a number
Converts the string `"10"` to the number 10, with ToNumber
trap: The establish–convert pair. Anyone who learned that "the `>` operator converts the string" tends to put the conversion first, as if it were unconditional. It is not: with two strings (`"10" > "9"`) there is no conversion at all and the comparison is lexicographic, returning `false`. It is establishing the types that decides which of the two comparisons will happen, which is why it comes first.

prompt: Match each expression to what it returns. There are options left over in the right-hand column.
hint: One of these results is a historical defect in the language, preserved for compatibility. Another surprises anyone expecting the value's name to describe its type.

prompt: In `0 == "0"` the result is `true`, but in `0 === "0"` it is `false`. What explains the difference?
hint: One of the two operators has an extra step before comparing. What step would that be, and what does it do to the string?

choices.text: `==` converts the operands to a common type before comparing; `===` compares type and value without converting anything.
choices.why: It is the difference between abstract and strict equality: the first applies coercion, the second fails immediately when the types differ.

choices.text: `==` compares only the textual content of the values, ignoring whether they are a number or a string.
choices.why: There is no textual comparison: `0 == "0"` is true because the string becomes the number 0, not because `0` and `"0"` look alike written down.

choices.text: `===` only works between primitive values, so with a string it returns `false` because it cannot compare them.
choices.why: `===` works with any value, strings included; it returns `false` here because the types are different.

choices.text: `==` rounds numbers before comparing, and the rounding makes `0` coincide with the string.
choices.why: No rounding is involved: the conversion is from string to number, and `"0"` is already exactly 0.

prompt: Tick every value that is **falsy** in JavaScript — that is, that behaves like `false` inside an `if`.
hint: The list of falsy values is closed and short. An empty object is still an object; an empty string is not the same thing as a string with one character in it.

choices.why: Zero is one of the values on the closed falsy list.
An empty string is falsy; any string with at least one character is truthy.
`NaN` is falsy, even though `typeof NaN` is `"number"`.
Every object is truthy, and an array is an object — even an empty one. It is the classic trap: `[] == false` is `true`, but `if ([])` runs.
It is a one-character string, therefore truthy. Only the empty string is falsy.
